name: Gum contouring laser
lead: Laser gum contouring is a dental procedure that uses a laser to remove and reshape gum tissue, a laser form of gingivectomy.[1] It is used to improve a smile by shortening gum that covers too much of the teeth, evening out an uneven gum line, or exposing more tooth crown, so that teeth look longer and better proportioned.[1][2]

The most common appearance reason is a gummy smile, in which too much gum shows above the upper teeth. Showing up to about 3 mm of gum when smiling is considered acceptable, and more than that is often seen as unattractive.[1] Excessive gingival display affects an estimated 10 percent of US adults aged 20 to 30 and is more common in women, with causes including delayed passive eruption of the teeth, an overactive upper lip elevator muscle, excessive vertical growth of the upper jaw and over-eruption of the front teeth.[2]

Common dental lasers are Nd:YAG, CO2 and diode lasers, with Er:YAG also used in crown lengthening trials.[1][3] Proponents say lasers give a bloodless field, minimal pain and swelling and no need for a surgical dressing, while the evidence comparing lasers with the scalpel is described as mixed.[1]

chain: Laser trims excess or uneven gum tissue
Teeth are exposed to their proper length and the gum line is even
angle.text: The procedure changes the visible gum line directly. When the gummy look comes from gum overgrowth or tissue covering the crowns, removing it makes the teeth look taller and brings the smile into a more balanced proportion.

infobox: Reduce gum display; even the gum line
Up to about 3 mm when smiling[1]
Orthodontics, botulinum toxin, fat transplantation, lip repositioning[2]

paras: Gingivectomy is described as the oldest surgical approach in periodontal therapy, cutting away part of the gum tissue to improve aesthetics or the long-term prognosis of teeth.[1] With a laser, the tissue is removed by repeated lasing with gauze wiping of debris, producing a bloodless field.[1] Other techniques are the scalpel and electrosurgery, the latter used less widely because of cost.[1]

Because of the potential for 'black triangles' and uneven gum contours, surgeons may treat a wider area, for example all teeth between the first molars, to keep the gum line harmonious.[1] The procedure is not appropriate when bone surgery is needed.[1]

A gummy smile can come from several causes, and treatment depends on which applies: orthodontic intrusion of the front teeth, gingivectomy, botulinum toxin into the upper lip elevator muscles, and micro-autologous fat transplantation are listed options.[2] Botox, which reduces upward lip movement so less gum shows, lasts about six months on average.[2]

Lasers are suggested to reduce bacteria, reduce inflammation, help healing and cause minimal swelling, bleeding, scarring or pain, and patients report minimal pain.[1] In animal studies Nd:YAG lasers healed better than scalpel incisions at low energy settings.[1] One study found minimal or no recurrence of drug-induced overgrowth after laser gingivectomy compared with scalpel gingivectomy.[1]

Conventional gingivectomy results are generally stable in drug-induced gingival enlargement, where most patients showed no recurrence after one year, while in hereditary gingival fibromatosis aesthetic results are good but recurrence is unpredictable and repeat procedures may be needed.[1]

High energy settings in animal studies caused scarring and delayed healing.[1] Pain is usually short-lived and manageable, patients avoid chewing on the area early on, and strict plaque control and regular professional cleaning are needed for lasting results; poor plaque control makes recurrence more likely.[1]

Registered trials include a phase 2 study of growth factor levels during wound healing after soft tissue crown lengthening (n=80, completed)[4] and a comparison of Er:YAG laser versus surgical crown lengthening (n=26, recruiting).[3] No results are summarised in the registrations.

card.summary: Laser removal of gum tissue to reshape the gum line; a laser variant of gingivectomy with little direct study.
card.note: Benefits over scalpel are based on limited evidence.

quick.overview:
A dental laser trims gum tissue to change the gum line. It is a laser version of gingivectomy.

The source material is thin; claims of less pain and bleeding rest on limited evidence.
quick.mechanism: The laser vaporizes and cuts soft tissue while sealing small vessels.
quick.risks: High energy settings were linked to scarring and delayed healing in animal studies.
